entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Fushimi Inari Taisha is Japan's most famous Shinto shrine and the head shrine of approximately 32,000 Inari shrines across Japan, located in Fushimi Ward, Kyoto. Famous for its thousands of vermilion torii gates creating tunnels of color through the sacred Mount Inari, it is dedicated to Inari Okami, the Shinto deity of foxes, rice, fertility, agriculture, industry, and worldly success.

Founded in 711 CE — though the deity's worship predates this date — Fushimi Inari Taisha became associated with rice cultivation and food production under the Empress Genmei, who ordered the shrine's establishment on Inariyama (Mount Inari). The shrine gained imperial patronage during the Heian period (794-1185 CE) when Kyoto became Japan's capital. The shrine's fox (kitsune) messengers, depicted in stone guardian statues throughout the complex, are considered the divine messengers of Inari.

The iconic rows of vermilion torii gates — totaling approximately 10,000 — were donated by individual worshippers and businesses since the Edo period (1603-1868 CE), each bearing the donor's name. Visiting businesses donate torii praying for commercial success, creating a living record of Japanese merchant culture. The mountain trail to the summit (4.5 km) passes numerous sub-shrines and takes 2-3 hours. Fushimi Inari is Japan's most-visited tourist destination, receiving 10+ million visitors annually.
